name: Corset tightlacing

lead: Tightlacing is the practice of lacing a corset increasingly tight over months or years to shrink the waistline and exaggerate an hourglass figure. It peaked in the 19th century and has been revived in alternative fashion and waist-training communities.

Wearers describe a dramatically smaller waist and upright posture while the corset is on. Medical commentators from the 1840s onward warned of harms, and skeletal studies of historical remains show rib and spine changes in habitual corset wearers.

paras: Practitioners move gradually to smaller or more tightly laced corsets and wear them for long periods, some including sleep, according to historical accounts. Modern waist training usually describes shorter daily wear than historical tightlacing.

Nineteenth-century physicians documented fainting, reduced breathing capacity and digestive problems, and bioarchaeological work reports skeletal deformation in long-term wearers. Many wearers reported little harm, according to historical sources. Anyone with a medical condition would be advised to consult a clinician.

chain: Waist compressed and torso shaped over time
angle.text: A tightly laced corset immediately narrows the visible waist, and long-term wearers say the effect carries over partly when it is removed. It is used for fashion, costume and waist-training aesthetics.

lead: Tightlacing, also called corset training, is the practice of wearing an increasingly tight corset to reshape the figure, mainly by reducing the waist [1][2]. It began in mid-19th-century Europe after steel eyelets, introduced in 1827, let corsets be laced much tighter without tearing [1].

Practitioners seek a narrow waist and hourglass silhouette; supporters have also valued an upright posture. Accounts describe reductions from about 23 inches to between 13 and 19 inches, and modern practitioners such as Cathie Jung have reported waists around 15 inches [1]. Historian David Kunzle suggested the practice was most common among middle and lower-middle-class women hoping to raise their social standing [1].

Physicians criticized it widely from the 1840s onward [3][4][5], and dress reformers promoted looser health corsets [1]. Corsets declined in the 1910s and 1920s and later reappeared in alternative fashion, with renewed interest in the 21st century [1]. Research is largely historical; no controlled modern studies of tightlacing were found.

paras: Tightlacing emphasizes extreme constriction rather than routine supportive corset wear; Grokipedia describes modern waist training as typically milder and intermittent by comparison [2]. Training reportedly began in childhood or adolescence for some Victorian girls, with progressively smaller corsets over months or years [1].

Laced bodices and stays existed from the Renaissance [2]. Tightlacing intensified in the 19th century, was mocked in satirical cartoons and became a target for doctors and dress reformers. Some physicians became corsetmakers, marketing health corsets with elastic panels [1].

Period medical writing includes an 1846 article on morbid effects of tight-lacing [3], an 1860 dental journal article on its evils [5], an 1887 report of an alarming result [6], an 1889 editorial on its effects [4], and a 1901 article linking tight-lacing and cycling to a displaced kidney [7].

A 2012 paleopathology paper discusses skeletal deformations from binding practices, including corseting, within a study of control over women's bodies [8]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports flattened ribs and spinal curvature in 18th- and 19th-century remains and notes that severity varied [2].
On T Nation one poster mentioned finding tightlacing attractive while doubting it is healthy [9].
No studies found. Historical medical articles and bioarchaeological work exist, but no modern clinical trials.
